screens.title: Unraveling Distributed Traces with OpenTelemetry
screens.narratorSegment: In modern microservices, a single user action often triggers many services, databases, and queues. Distributed tracing gives you a coherent, end-to-end picture of that single request so you can find where time is spent and where failures occur. In this lesson we will learn the essential terms — traces, spans, and context propagation — and then see how OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral set of SDKs, a Collector, and exporters to capture and route that data. You will also learn practical instrumentation patterns: when to rely on auto-instrumentation, when to add manual spans, and how sampling and attributes keep trace volume manageable. A concrete example in this chapter shows two Python Flask services, a Collector, and Jaeger for visualizing traces. We will walk through initializing the SDK, creating spans for a payment flow, and avoiding common mistakes like broken context or excessive span creation. By the end you will be able to explain why tracing is the most direct way to answer “which service slowed my request” and how to set up OTel to capture that signal without locking into a backend. Think about a recent outage you investigated — this lesson will help you turn that time-sink into a fast diagnosis.

screens.title: What is Distributed Tracing?
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed tracing is the practice of recording the execution path of a single logical request as it flows across multiple services. At a basic level it answers the question: what sequence of operations and services did this request touch, and how much time did each step take? Think of a trace as a recorded flight path for one passenger: each span is like a flight segment between waypoints, with timestamps and metadata about the plane’s conditions. In practice, spans include an operation name, start and end times, attributes for context, events for notable moments, and a parent reference to reconstruct the hierarchy. This matters because when a user experiences a slow A P I or an intermittent error, aggregated metrics may not reveal the specific chain of calls that produced the failure. A single trace, however, will show the slow span—the long pole—and reveal whether the delay was a database query, an external A P I call, or an internal retry loop. A common misconception is that tracing replaces logs; it does not. Traces complement logs by showing causal relationships and precise timings. Key takeaway: tracing gives you a timeline for one transaction, enabling targeted root cause analysis instead of broad, blind digging.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is Distributed Tracing?
Definition and analogy
Distributed tracing records a single request’s path across services. Imagine tracking a passenger’s flights; each leg is a span with start and end times and data about that leg.
Span data
  • Operation Name: human-friendly label
  • Timestamps: start and end to measure duration
  • Attributes: key-value context
  • Parent ID: links to caller span
Common uses
Find long-running calls, follow errors across boundaries, and validate that retries or timeouts occur where expected.
Analogy
Flight legs for a passenger; trace is entire itinerary.
Misconception
Tracing replaces logs — no. Use both to diagnose issues effectively.
Key takeaway
Traces reveal causal timing across services so you can find the true bottleneck quickly.
Concrete example
A slow API request shows a 500ms database query span; tracing points to the query as the long pole, not the frontend or network.
Key Takeaway

Tracing gives a single-request timeline that isolates which operation causes latency or failures.

screens.title: Traces, Spans, and Span Metadata
screens.narratorSegment: A trace is a tree or waterfall of spans. Each span represents a single timed unit of work: an HTTP request, a database query, or a message publish/consume. Spans are hierarchical: a parent span is the operation that triggered child spans. That parent-child relationship is built using a parent span ID and a shared trace ID so all spans for a request can be linked. Each span carries metadata that makes analysis practical. The operation name is human-readable, such as GET /users/{id} or authenticateUser. Start and end timestamps compute duration. Attributes provide contextual key-value pairs like http. status_code, db. statement, or user_id. Events attach time-stamped notes for points of interest, such as retries or errors. When you inspect a trace in a visualization tool, you typically see a waterfall timeline where spans line up by start time. Look for unusually long spans or blocks of time where child spans are waiting on a parent to finish; these are the long-pole patterns. A common misconception is that more attributes are always better — excess attributes increase overhead and can leak sensitive data. Be selective and prefer adding high-value attributes and occasional events over verbose payload dumps. Can you identify which attribute will help you triage a slow request in your system?

keyIdea.text: Spans hold operation names, timestamps, attributes, events, and parent references. Together they form a trace that exposes timing and causality.

content.html:
Definition › Traces & Spans
Span metadata breakdown
Each span carries the data you need to diagnose behavior and measure latency. Use attributes for structured context and events for notable timestamps.
Operation Name
Human readable label to identify the unit of work.
Timestamps
Start and end time produce span duration used for waterfall analysis.
Attributes & Events
Key-value context and logged events that enrich a span for triage.
Hierarchy visualization
A parent span can have many children. Visual tools show this as a nested or waterfall timeline so relationships are clear.
Example span attributes
  • http.method: GET
  • http.status_code: 200
  • db.statement: SELECT id FROM users WHERE id = ?
  • user.id: 42 (redact in production if PII)
Key takeaway
Select attributes that help root cause analysis while avoiding sensitive or excessive data.
Quick check
When you see a slow trace, look for the single longest span or an unexpected sequence of waiting child spans.

screens.title: Context Propagation: Keeping Traces Intact
screens.narratorSegment: Context propagation is the mechanism that keeps spans from breaking into isolated fragments when a request crosses service boundaries. Without propagation, each service would create an independent root span and traces would look incomplete. The usual pattern is simple: when a service makes an outgoing request, it injects the current trace context — including the trace ID and the caller span ID — into request headers or message metadata. The receiving service extracts that context and creates a child span that references the incoming span as its parent. W3C Trace Context defines standard headers like traceparent and tracestate for HTTP, but message queues use message headers for the same purpose. A practical example is an HTTP frontend calling a backend: the frontend’s TracerProvider ensures RequestsInstrumentor injects the traceparent header; the backend’s FlaskInstrumentor reads it, continues the same trace, and creates spans that show a linked waterfall. A common misconception is that propagation is automatic across every library; instrumentors are required or you must manually inject and extract context for custom clients. Key takeaway: ensure every outbound client and inbound server path is instrumented or manually propagates context to avoid broken traces and missing links.

keyIdea.title: Propagation summary
keyIdea.text: Trace and span IDs must be injected into outgoing requests and extracted by receivers. Standard headers or message attributes maintain the trace chain.

content.html:
Process Flow › Context Propagation
How propagation works
Propagation injects trace identifiers into outgoing calls and extracts them when a service receives a call so child spans link to the original trace.
HTTP example
Inject the traceparent header on the client. The server extracts it and creates a child span with parent span ID set to the caller.
Message queues
Put trace context in message headers so consumer services can continue the same trace when processing.
Gotcha
If a custom HTTP client or queue library is not instrumented, you must manually inject and extract context to avoid broken traces.
Concrete scenario
A frontend requests backend. RequestsInstrumentor injects trace headers; FlaskInstrumentor on the backend extracts them and creates child spans that appear linked in Jaeger.
Key Takeaway

Propagation preserves trace continuity. Missing instrumentation on any link breaks the trace into fragments.

screens.title: OpenTelemetry: A Vendor-Neutral Observability Framework
screens.narratorSegment: OpenTelemetry is an open, vendor-neutral framework that standardizes how applications produce telemetry: traces, metrics, and logs. The key benefit is decoupling instrumentation from the choice of backend. Before OpenTelemetry, teams often reached for a vendor-specific client and became tied to a particular tracing backend. With OTel, you instrument once using a common A P I and can later export to Jaeger, Zipkin, or a commercial service without changing the instrumentation code. The Collector acts as a central agent or gateway: it receives OTLP data, applies processors such as batching or filtering, and sends the result to one or more exporters. This reduces load on application services and centralizes configuration like sampling rules. The SDKs are language specific and provide the APIs for creating spans, propagating context, and registering exporters. A common misconception is that OpenTelemetry itself stores or visualizes traces; it does not — the Collector and an external backend provide storage and UI. OpenTelemetry’s strength is in providing consistent, portable telemetry that teams can adapt to evolving backend preferences while keeping instrumentation stable. OpenTelemetry: A Vendor-Neutral Observability Framework means opentelemetry provides sdks, a collector, and standard protocols so you can instrument once and export telemetry to multiple backends without vendor lock-in.. In practical terms, why a standard api and collector matter for instrumentation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › OpenTelemetry
OpenTelemetry components
OTel provides APIs and SDKs for multiple languages, a Collector to process telemetry, and exporters to send data to tracing backends. Instrumentation becomes portable and configurable.
SDKs
Language libraries that create spans and handle propagation.
Collector
Central agent that receives, processes, and exports telemetry.
Backends
Visualization and storage systems like Jaeger or Zipkin accept exported traces.
Remember: OTel standardizes how you generate telemetry but does not store or display traces itself. That is the job of a tracing backend connected to the Collector.
Concrete benefit
Instrument a service once and change the backend later without touching business code. This reduces lock-in and operational churn.
Key Takeaway

OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral bridge between instrumented code and any tracing backend you choose.

screens.title: An OpenTelemetry Tracing Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: A typical OpenTelemetry tracing pipeline has three main layers. First, application code uses language SDKs that create spans and propagate context. These SDKs may be auto-instrumentors or manual APIs for creating custom spans. Second, the OpenTelemetry Collector sits between apps and your backends. It receives OTLP data, applies processors such as batching, sampling, or attribute enrichment, and exports data to one or more backends. The Collector can run as an agent next to the application or as a centralized gateway. Its key benefit is offloading export and processing work from application services. Third, tracing backends store and visualize traces and provide query and dependency maps. In practice you might deploy a Collector that sends traces to Jaeger and a logging exporter for debugging. Important operational choices include where to run the Collector, how aggressive sampling should be, and whether to add processors that redact or enrich attributes. A common misconception is that pushing raw, unfiltered telemetry to all backends is harmless; in reality it multiplies storage costs and can expose sensitive data. The architectural answer is to centralize processing in the Collector, apply sensible sampling and redaction, then forward curated telemetry to the right backend.

Architecture › OTel Pipeline
Pipeline layers
SDKs produce telemetry locally; the Collector receives, processes, and exports; backends store and visualize traces. Use processors to filter, batch, and enrich data before export.
SDKs
Auto-instrumentation and manual APIs in each service language.
Collector
Receives OTLP, applies processors (sampling, redaction), and exports to backends.
Backends
Jaeger, Zipkin, or commercial UIs for searching and waterfall views.
Operational decisions: run Collector as sidecar or gateway, set sampling rates per pipeline, and choose processors to redact or enrich attributes centrally.
Concrete decision
Run the Collector centrally to reduce configuration in apps and to centralize sampling and redaction rules for consistent, safe telemetry.
Key Takeaway

The Collector is the right place to manage trace volume and privacy before exporting to backends.

screens.title: Auto-Instrumentation vs Manual Spans
screens.narratorSegment: Auto-instrumentation gives quick coverage: many frameworks and HTTP clients can be instrumented without changing application code. For example, using FlaskInstrumentor or RequestsInstrumentor will automatically create spans for incoming HTTP requests and outgoing calls. This is the fastest way to get meaningful traces across a system. Manual instrumentation, however, is for business-critical logic you want to highlight or measure precisely. Manual spans let you add attributes, events, and status codes at meaningful boundaries. The trade-off is overhead: creating too many manual spans or making every small function a span generates trace noise and increases storage and processing. The recommended pattern is hybrid: use auto-instrumentation for framework-level traces and add manual child spans only for significant operations like payment processing, database migrations, or external A P I calls where extra context matters. A common mistake is creating new root spans for internal calls rather than child spans; this fragments traces and makes analysis harder. Another mistake is over-instrumenting non-critical loops. Key takeaway: start with auto-instrumentation for broad visibility, then add targeted manual spans and attributes to capture high-value business context. Auto-Instrumentation vs Manual Spans means use auto-instrumentation for coverage; supplement with manual child spans for important business operations to balance cost and signal.. In practical terms, trade-offs, when to use each, and a recommended hybrid approach. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Assuming every library is instrumented; custom calls may need manual context handling.
Manual spans
Pros: precise control, add business attributes and events. Cons: overhead if overused.
Use when
Important business logic such as payment processing or complex orchestration.
Pitfall
Creating root spans for internal calls rather than child spans, which breaks trace continuity.
Key Takeaway

Adopt a hybrid approach: auto-instrument widely, add manual child spans for high-value operations, avoid excessive span creation.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › SDK Initialization
Example initialization (Python)
<!-- Escaped Python example -->
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter

resource = Resource.create({"service.name": "my-payment-service"})
provider = TracerProvider(resource=resource)
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(OTLPSpanExporter(endpoint="localhost:4317")))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)
This snippet shows the minimal setup: a service name resource, a TracerProvider, and an OTLP exporter pointing to the Collector. Use a BatchSpanProcessor in production for performance.
Concrete guidance
Set the resource with service.name, use BatchSpanProcessor for production, and confirm spans appear in Jaeger when the Collector is running.
Common mistake
Initializing the tracer after requests begin can result in missing spans. Initialize at process startup.
Key Takeaway

Initialize your TracerProvider early, export to the Collector, and prefer batch processing for production workloads.

screens.narratorSegment: When auto-instrumentation does not capture critical business logic, create manual spans around important operations. The chapter example shows a process_payment function that opens a span named process_payment_logic, sets attributes like payment. amount and payment. currency, sleeps to simulate work, and adds an event when the payment gateway request is sent. Creating child spans like this keeps important details in the trace without over-instrumenting. Note how the code uses the tracer. start_as_current_span context manager so the span is active for nested operations and will be exported with proper parent linkage. Also observe the span. set_status call on error to mark a span as failed, which surfaces clearly in the tracing UI. A common misconception is to create root spans for each function; instead, these should be child spans inside the request’s root span created by the web framework. Code Walkthrough › Manual Span Example
Manual span example (Python)
# --- Manual Span Creation ---
from opentelemetry import trace
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

def process_payment(amount, currency):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("process_payment_logic") as span:
        span.set_attribute("payment.amount", amount)
        span.set_attribute("payment.currency", currency)
        import time
        time.sleep(0.1)
        span.add_event("payment_gateway_request_sent", {"gateway": "stripe"})
        if amount > 1000:
            span.set_status(trace.Status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR, "Payment too large"))
            raise ValueError("Payment amount exceeds limit")
        return "Payment successful"
This code shows the pattern: open a span, set attributes for context, add events for external calls, and set error status on exceptions so the backend highlights failures.
Concrete note
Use child spans so the payment logic appears within the HTTP request's trace. Avoid creating standalone roots for internal functions.
Common mistake
Adding sensitive data like full request payloads as attributes. Sanitize or omit PII before adding attributes.
Key Takeaway

Manual spans add business context. Use them sparingly, as children of the request span, and avoid leaking sensitive attributes.

screens.title: Common Mistakes, Performance, and Security
screens.narratorSegment: Three operational pitfalls are worth calling out: incomplete instrumentation, excessive span creation, and leaking sensitive data. Incomplete instrumentation is when some services or clients are not instrumented or when custom clients do not inject or extract trace context. This causes broken traces and forces guesswork when performing root cause analysis. Excessive instrumentation means creating spans for every small function call. Each span adds C P U, memory, network, and storage overhead and can overwhelm your backend and increase costs. The better approach is to create child spans around significant operations and use attributes or events for lightweight context. Sampling is your friend: trace a percentage of requests in production to reduce volume while preserving signal. Finally, security: trace attributes might contain PII or internal architecture details. Sanitize attributes and restrict backend access to trusted users. The Collector is the right place to centralize sampling and redaction to ensure consistency. Key takeaway: instrument comprehensively but selectively, use sampling to manage volume, and protect sensitive data by centralizing redaction in the Collector. Common Mistakes › Performance & Security
Incomplete instrumentation
If any link does not propagate context, traces break. Ensure custom clients inject and extract trace headers or use instrumented libraries.
Excessive span creation
Too many spans create noise and overhead. Prefer child spans for key operations and attributes/events for lightweight context. Use sampling to limit volume.
Sensitive data
Traces can reveal internal architecture or user data. Sanitize attributes and centralize redaction in the Collector. Limit backend access.
Pro tip
Use the Collector to implement consistent sampling and redaction rules so apps remain simple and safe.
Key Takeaway

Instrument broadly but selectively, control volume with sampling, and centralize privacy rules in the Collector to keep tracing safe and efficient.

screens.title: Using Traces to Diagnose Latency and Failures
screens.narratorSegment: When diagnosing intermittent latency, traces reveal patterns you cannot see in aggregated metrics. Two useful patterns are the long-pole and parent-wait. The long-pole pattern shows a single unusually long span in the waterfall; that span is the immediate suspect and often corresponds to a slow database query or external A P I. The parent-wait pattern occurs when many child spans are idle waiting for a parent to complete, which may indicate blocking input and output or synchronous work in the parent. To apply these patterns, find a slow user request trace in Jaeger and examine the waterfall: look for spans whose duration is far outside the baseline and observe whether child spans are shifted in time. Also inspect attributes: an http. status_code or db. statement may confirm the nature of the operation. Use sampling to capture a representative set of traces for intermittent issues; capturing only a single slow trace risks chasing a rare outlier. A common misconception is to rely solely on averages; traces show per-request behavior and reveal tail latency. Key takeaway: use the waterfall and span attributes to find the long pole or parent-wait, then drill into the responsible service and operation for remediation.

content.html:
Troubleshooting › Diagnosing Latency
Diagnostic patterns
When you have an intermittent slow request, open a trace and inspect the waterfall. A single long span points to the long pole; many children waiting points to parent-wait or blocking work.
Long-pole
Identify one span much longer than others. That operation is the top candidate for optimization.
Parent-wait
Child spans appear delayed because the parent is blocking; investigate synchronous operations in the parent span.
Inspect attributes on the suspicious spans — database statements, status codes, and custom attributes — to confirm the source. Use a handful of sampled slow traces to validate patterns rather than one example trace to avoid chasing a fluke.
Concrete example
A trace shows a backend database span taking 500ms while others take 20ms. The long-pole pattern points you to optimize the query or add an index.
Key Takeaway

Traces let you find per-request tail latency patterns—the long pole or parent-wait—so you can target the precise operation to fix.

fullNarratorScript:
In modern microservices, a single user action often triggers many services, databases, and queues. Distributed tracing gives you a coherent, end-to-end picture of that single request so you can find where time is spent and where failures occur. In this lesson we will learn the essential terms — traces, spans, and context propagation — and then see how OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral set of SDKs, a Collector, and exporters to capture and route that data. You will also learn practical instrumentation patterns: when to rely on auto-instrumentation, when to add manual spans, and how sampling and attributes keep trace volume manageable. A concrete example in this chapter shows two Python Flask services, a Collector, and Jaeger for visualizing traces. We will walk through initializing the SDK, creating spans for a payment flow, and avoiding common mistakes like broken context or excessive span creation. By the end you will be able to explain why tracing is the most direct way to answer “which service slowed my request” and how to set up OTel to capture that signal without locking into a backend. Think about a recent outage you investigated — this lesson will help you turn that time-sink into a fast diagnosis.

By the end of this chapter you will define distributed tracing and explain why it is essential for debugging and performance in microservices. You will understand traces and spans: how spans carry timestamps, operation names, attributes, events, and parent references. You will be able to describe context propagation and the mechanics of passing trace IDs between services, including the idea behind W3C Trace Context headers. You will also explain OpenTelemetry’s role as a vendor-neutral standard and name its primary components: SDKs for instrumenting code, the Collector for processing telemetry, and tracing backends like Jaeger for visualization. Distributed tracing is the practice of recording the execution path of a single logical request as it flows across multiple services. At a basic level it answers the question: what sequence of operations and services did this request touch, and how much time did each step take? Think of a trace as a recorded flight path for one passenger: each span is like a flight segment between waypoints, with timestamps and metadata about the plane’s conditions. In practice, spans include an operation name, start and end times, attributes for context, events for notable moments, and a parent reference to reconstruct the hierarchy. This matters because when a user experiences a slow A P I or an intermittent error, aggregated metrics may not reveal the specific chain of calls that produced the failure. A single trace, however, will show the slow span—the long pole—and reveal whether the delay was a database query, an external A P I call, or an internal retry loop. A common misconception is that tracing replaces logs; it does not. Traces complement logs by showing causal relationships and precise timings. Key takeaway: tracing gives you a timeline for one transaction, enabling targeted root cause analysis instead of broad, blind digging.

A trace is a tree or waterfall of spans. Each span represents a single timed unit of work: an HTTP request, a database query, or a message publish/consume. Spans are hierarchical: a parent span is the operation that triggered child spans. That parent-child relationship is built using a parent span ID and a shared trace ID so all spans for a request can be linked. Each span carries metadata that makes analysis practical. The operation name is human-readable, such as GET /users/{id} or authenticateUser. Start and end timestamps compute duration. Attributes provide contextual key-value pairs like http. status_code, db. statement, or user_id. Events attach time-stamped notes for points of interest, such as retries or errors. When you inspect a trace in a visualization tool, you typically see a waterfall timeline where spans line up by start time. Look for unusually long spans or blocks of time where child spans are waiting on a parent to finish; these are the long-pole patterns. A common misconception is that more attributes are always better — excess attributes increase overhead and can leak sensitive data. Be selective and prefer adding high-value attributes and occasional events over verbose payload dumps. Can you identify which attribute will help you triage a slow request in your system?

Context propagation is the mechanism that keeps spans from breaking into isolated fragments when a request crosses service boundaries. Without propagation, each service would create an independent root span and traces would look incomplete. The usual pattern is simple: when a service makes an outgoing request, it injects the current trace context — including the trace ID and the caller span ID — into request headers or message metadata. The receiving service extracts that context and creates a child span that references the incoming span as its parent. W3C Trace Context defines standard headers like traceparent and tracestate for HTTP, but message queues use message headers for the same purpose. A practical example is an HTTP frontend calling a backend: the frontend’s TracerProvider ensures RequestsInstrumentor injects the traceparent header; the backend’s FlaskInstrumentor reads it, continues the same trace, and creates spans that show a linked waterfall. A common misconception is that propagation is automatic across every library; instrumentors are required or you must manually inject and extract context for custom clients. Key takeaway: ensure every outbound client and inbound server path is instrumented or manually propagates context to avoid broken traces and missing links.

OpenTelemetry is an open, vendor-neutral framework that standardizes how applications produce telemetry: traces, metrics, and logs. The key benefit is decoupling instrumentation from the choice of backend. Before OpenTelemetry, teams often reached for a vendor-specific client and became tied to a particular tracing backend. With OTel, you instrument once using a common A P I and can later export to Jaeger, Zipkin, or a commercial service without changing the instrumentation code. The Collector acts as a central agent or gateway: it receives OTLP data, applies processors such as batching or filtering, and sends the result to one or more exporters. This reduces load on application services and centralizes configuration like sampling rules. The SDKs are language specific and provide the APIs for creating spans, propagating context, and registering exporters. A common misconception is that OpenTelemetry itself stores or visualizes traces; it does not — the Collector and an external backend provide storage and UI. OpenTelemetry’s strength is in providing consistent, portable telemetry that teams can adapt to evolving backend preferences while keeping instrumentation stable. A typical OpenTelemetry tracing pipeline has three main layers. First, application code uses language SDKs that create spans and propagate context. These SDKs may be auto-instrumentors or manual APIs for creating custom spans. Second, the OpenTelemetry Collector sits between apps and your backends. It receives OTLP data, applies processors such as batching, sampling, or attribute enrichment, and exports data to one or more backends. The Collector can run as an agent next to the application or as a centralized gateway. Its key benefit is offloading export and processing work from application services. Third, tracing backends store and visualize traces and provide query and dependency maps. In practice you might deploy a Collector that sends traces to Jaeger and a logging exporter for debugging. Important operational choices include where to run the Collector, how aggressive sampling should be, and whether to add processors that redact or enrich attributes. A common misconception is that pushing raw, unfiltered telemetry to all backends is harmless; in reality it multiplies storage costs and can expose sensitive data. The architectural answer is to centralize processing in the Collector, apply sensible sampling and redaction, then forward curated telemetry to the right backend.

Auto-instrumentation gives quick coverage: many frameworks and HTTP clients can be instrumented without changing application code. For example, using FlaskInstrumentor or RequestsInstrumentor will automatically create spans for incoming HTTP requests and outgoing calls. This is the fastest way to get meaningful traces across a system. Manual instrumentation, however, is for business-critical logic you want to highlight or measure precisely. Manual spans let you add attributes, events, and status codes at meaningful boundaries. The trade-off is overhead: creating too many manual spans or making every small function a span generates trace noise and increases storage and processing. The recommended pattern is hybrid: use auto-instrumentation for framework-level traces and add manual child spans only for significant operations like payment processing, database migrations, or external A P I calls where extra context matters. A common mistake is creating new root spans for internal calls rather than child spans; this fragments traces and makes analysis harder. Another mistake is over-instrumenting non-critical loops. Key takeaway: start with auto-instrumentation for broad visibility, then add targeted manual spans and attributes to capture high-value business context. In development you might export to the console to inspect spans locally, while in production you use BatchSpanProcessor and OTLP to reduce overhead and send traces reliably. When auto-instrumentation does not capture critical business logic, create manual spans around important operations. The chapter example shows a process_payment function that opens a span named process_payment_logic, sets attributes like payment. amount and payment. currency, sleeps to simulate work, and adds an event when the payment gateway request is sent. Creating child spans like this keeps important details in the trace without over-instrumenting. Note how the code uses the tracer. start_as_current_span context manager so the span is active for nested operations and will be exported with proper parent linkage. Also observe the span. set_status call on error to mark a span as failed, which surfaces clearly in the tracing UI. A common misconception is to create root spans for each function; instead, these should be child spans inside the request’s root span created by the web framework. Use attributes for structured data and events for notable moments, reserving full payloads for exceptional cases and ensuring sensitive fields are removed. Key takeaway: manual spans provide high-value detail when used sparingly and as children of the request span. This hands-on activity shows the end-to-end steps to observe a trace across two services. Start the Collector and Jaeger using the provided docker-compose file. Next, instrument both frontend and backend Python services: initialize the TracerProvider, add an OTLP exporter pointed at the Collector, and run RequestsInstrumentor and FlaskInstrumentor so HTTP spans are created automatically. Key takeaway: follow the pipeline from code to Collector to Jaeger to ensure traces are being created, propagated, and visualized end-to-end.

Three operational pitfalls are worth calling out: incomplete instrumentation, excessive span creation, and leaking sensitive data. Incomplete instrumentation is when some services or clients are not instrumented or when custom clients do not inject or extract trace context. This causes broken traces and forces guesswork when performing root cause analysis. Excessive instrumentation means creating spans for every small function call. Each span adds C P U, memory, network, and storage overhead and can overwhelm your backend and increase costs. The better approach is to create child spans around significant operations and use attributes or events for lightweight context. Sampling is your friend: trace a percentage of requests in production to reduce volume while preserving signal. Finally, security: trace attributes might contain PII or internal architecture details. Sanitize attributes and restrict backend access to trusted users. The Collector is the right place to centralize sampling and redaction to ensure consistency. Key takeaway: instrument comprehensively but selectively, use sampling to manage volume, and protect sensitive data by centralizing redaction in the Collector. When diagnosing intermittent latency, traces reveal patterns you cannot see in aggregated metrics. Two useful patterns are the long-pole and parent-wait. The long-pole pattern shows a single unusually long span in the waterfall; that span is the immediate suspect and often corresponds to a slow database query or external A P I. The parent-wait pattern occurs when many child spans are idle waiting for a parent to complete, which may indicate blocking input and output or synchronous work in the parent. To apply these patterns, find a slow user request trace in Jaeger and examine the waterfall: look for spans whose duration is far outside the baseline and observe whether child spans are shifted in time. Also inspect attributes: an http. status_code or db. statement may confirm the nature of the operation. Use sampling to capture a representative set of traces for intermittent issues; capturing only a single slow trace risks chasing a rare outlier. A common misconception is to rely solely on averages; traces show per-request behavior and reveal tail latency. Key takeaway: use the waterfall and span attributes to find the long pole or parent-wait, then drill into the responsible service and operation for remediation.

These three concept cards capture the essential ideas you should remember. First, distributed tracing tracks a single request across services using traces and spans to reveal timing and causality. Second, context propagation is required to link spans: inject trace headers on outgoing calls and extract them on incoming calls. Third, OpenTelemetry provides portable SDKs and a Collector so you can instrument once and export telemetry to different backends while centralizing processing, sampling, and redaction. Use auto-instrumentation to bootstrap coverage, add manual child spans for high-value business logic, and centralize volume and privacy controls at the Collector. These principles let you transform opaque distributed behavior into clear, actionable traces for debugging and performance tuning. Keep three practical reminders in mind as you instrument systems. First, always ensure propagation: missing context is the most common cause of broken traces. Second, be selective about spans and attributes: capture what helps triage and avoid sensitive or verbose fields. Third, centralize sampling and redaction in the Collector so your apps remain simple and policies remain consistent. These rules will help you scale tracing safely and ensure traces are useful for diagnosing latency and failures without overwhelming your systems or exposing private data.
